title: How do we do four subtractions with different bottom numbers?
description: Four subtractions are done by first changing each pair to the same bottom number, then taking away the tops, then writing the answer in lowest terms.
teaching_notes: One idea: change both fractions to the same bottom number, take away the tops and keep the bottom, then write the answer in lowest terms. Watch for students who take away the bottoms, or who change only one of the two fractions.

source: Carry out the following subtractions using Brahmagupta's method: a) 8/15 − 3/15 b) 2/5 − 4/15 c) 5/6 − 4/9 d) 2/3 − 1/2
video_script.why: The child changes each pair to the same bottom number, takes away the tops, and writes each answer in lowest terms, the way the book's solved question does.
video_script.substitution: The book's method for taking away fractions with different bottom numbers, used on four subtractions in a row.
video_script.anchor: four subtractions written in a row on the board, as in the book
video_script.payoff_line: The four answers are one third, two fifteenths, seven eighteenths and one sixth

final_answer.spoken: one third, two fifteenths, seven eighteenths and one sixth

video_script.fraction_reading: eight fifteenths, three fifteenths, two fifths, four fifteenths, five sixths, four ninths, two thirds, one half, one third, two fifteenths, seven eighteenths, one sixth
never_show: the four answers together in one line before the answer beat
video_script.design: One idea: same bottom number first, then take away the tops, then lowest terms. The four subtractions stay on the board as the anchor and each step works on one of them in order.

beats.on_screen: a small title card From your book; four subtractions in a row: 8/15 − 3/15, 2/5 − 4/15, 5/6 − 4/9, 2/3 − 1/2

marks.book: the small title card From your book appears
marks.list: the four subtractions appear one after another in a row
marks.ask: the bottom numbers of each pair glow in turn

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book, with four subtractions to do.
<bookmark mark='list'/>Eight fifteenths take away three fifteenths. Two fifths take away four fifteenths. Five sixths take away four ninths. Two thirds take away one half.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Some pairs have different bottom numbers. What must we do before we take away?

beats.on_screen: the four subtractions hold still and the question stays on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a strip showing 1/2 and a strip showing 1/4 side by side; the 1/2 strip is cut again to show 2/4; the words equivalent fractions

marks.sizes: the half and the quarter glow to show different sizes
marks.cut: the half is cut into two equal parts and 2/4 appears

narration: <bookmark mark='sizes'/>We can only take away parts of the same size. A half and a quarter are different sizes.
<bookmark mark='cut'/>Cut the half into two equal parts, and it becomes two quarters. Fractions equal in size are called equivalent fractions.
<bookmark mark='same'/>Then both count quarters, and we can take away the tops.

marks.given: the four subtractions are written on the working board

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, four subtractions, each to be done by changing to the same bottom number first.

marks.find: the words to find are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find all four answers.

marks.first: the first subtraction glows and the bottom number 15 is shown twice
marks.low: the words lowest terms appear with 5 and 15 glowing

narration: <bookmark mark='first'/>Step one, the first subtraction already has the same bottom number, fifteen. Take away the tops and keep the bottom.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Eight take away three is five, so we get five fifteenths.
<bookmark mark='low'/>Write it in lowest terms. Lowest terms means the top and the bottom share no factor except one.
<bookmark mark='div'/>Five and fifteen both divide by five, which gives one third.

marks.second: the second subtraction glows with the bottom numbers 5 and 15
marks.mult: the top 2 and the bottom 5 are each multiplied by 3 and 6/15 appears

narration: <bookmark mark='second'/>Step two, the second subtraction has fifths and fifteenths. Five times three is fifteen, so change the fifths into fifteenths.
<bookmark mark='mult'/>Multiply the top and the bottom of two fifths by three. This is the same way as the example in your book. That gives six fifteenths.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Six take away four is two, so we get two fifteenths. Two and fifteen share no factor except one.

marks.third: the third subtraction glows with the bottom numbers 6 and 9
marks.six: 5/6 becomes 15/18 with the multiplier 3 on the top and the bottom
marks.nine: 4/9 becomes 8/18 with the multiplier 2 on the top and the bottom

narration: <bookmark mark='third'/>Step three, the third subtraction has sixths and ninths. Six and nine both go into eighteen.
<bookmark mark='six'/>Multiply the top and the bottom of five sixths by three. That gives fifteen eighteenths.
<bookmark mark='nine'/>Multiply the top and the bottom of four ninths by two. That gives eight eighteenths.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Fifteen take away eight is seven, so we get seven eighteenths.

marks.fourth: the last subtraction glows with the bottom numbers 3 and 2
marks.thirds: 2/3 becomes 4/6 with the multiplier 2 on the top and the bottom
marks.half: 1/2 becomes 3/6 with the multiplier 3 on the top and the bottom

narration: <bookmark mark='fourth'/>Step four, the last subtraction has thirds and halves. Three and two both go into six.
<bookmark mark='thirds'/>Multiply two thirds by two on the top and the bottom. That gives four sixths.
<bookmark mark='half'/>Multiply one half by three on the top and the bottom. That gives three sixths.
<bookmark mark='take'/>Four take away three is one, so we get one sixth.

marks.back: each working answer slides back beside the fraction that was taken away
marks.add: the four sums appear and each one matches its starting fraction

narration: <bookmark mark='back'/>Step five, check by putting each answer back in its question.
<bookmark mark='add'/>Add each answer to the part we took away, and we get back the starting fraction every time.

marks.ans: the four answers 1/3, 2/15, 7/18, 1/6 are boxed in a row

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>The four answers are one third, two fifteenths, seven eighteenths and one sixth.
